Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

After Cai Guo-Qiang Quick, before the sun rises, get up one more time, my grandmother. The artist won’t mind if you borrow his sky ladder. Place your foot on the bottom rung and keep climbing, even though you’re a skeleton with a broken neck from falling downstairs on Guy Fawkes night. The ladder is wrapped in gunpowder, and he’s lit the touchpaper. Your bones are ascending firecrackers. You’re half a kilometer high now, halfway to the universe, my joy-gardener. I hope you find a garden with rich black soil for your black roses, hybrids like you— half white half Indian, half woman half flower, their roots twined through your skull, you who were transplanted among the pale roses of a British family. Your skin now a mix of photons and soot. What do you find up there? Is there a hothouse? Are there alien hands with deft brushes pollinating stars? Remember how your tomatoes kept yielding more planets? Are there constellations of exotic fruit now you’ve reached the top? Have you gone back enough in space-time to when you were alive? The ladder is charred, the hot air balloon that held it up is about to collapse. The explosions are over. Cai showers his head with champagne, as his 100-year-old granny watches on her cell phone.Did you see it? He asks,did you hear the whoosh, the rat-tat-tat at the starry door? You can go back to sleep now

Prior to daybreak, hurry to wake once more, grandmother, following the inspiration of Cai Guo-Qiang. The artist will gladly let you borrow his soaring staircase. Step onto the lowest rung and keep ascending, even though you are a skeletal frame whose neck snapped from a stairwell tumble on Bonfire Night. Packed with explosive propellant, the fuse on the structure has been lit, turning your bones into rising fireworks. You have elevated five hundred meters into the air—a midpoint toward outer space—my cultivator of happiness. 

May you discover a plot of rich, dark earth suited for your dark-hued roses. They share your own dual heritage—part Caucasian, part Indian, part female, and part botanical—their roots tangled inside your cranium, reflecting your relocation among the fair-complexioned roses of an English family. By now, your outer layer is a fusion of light particles and ash. 

What greets you at the peak? Is there a greenhouse up there? Do otherworldly fingers expertly wield brushes to cross-pollinate the stars? Recall how your tomato plants used to yield endless worlds; are there now starry clusters of unusual fruits at the summit? Have you traveled far enough backward through temporal space to return to your living self? 

Now blackened by fire, the ladder hangs beneath a collapsing hot-air vessel, and the pyrotechnic blasts have ceased. Cai douses his own head in sparkling wine while his centenarian grandmother observes the spectacle through a smartphone screen. He asks if she caught the sight, if she heard the rushing air and the rapid knocking against heaven's portal. You may return to your rest now.

Look up into the night, Grandmother, for the darkness is about to split wide open. Step close to the base of Cai Guo-Qiang’s grand creation as the fuse ignites, sending a streak of golden fire roaring toward the clouds. A ladder of pure light is tethered to the heavens, and I urge your spirit to take to its rungs. Climb beyond the atmosphere, leaving behind the heavy pull of the earth, and ride this blazing pathway straight into the cosmos.

As I watch the sparks ascend, I remember you as you were in life: a joy-bringing gardener whose quiet radiance illuminated every room. Yours was a rich, mixed-race heritage, a vibrant life transplanted into the structured soil of a traditional British family. Yet, like the rarest blooms, you took root with grace, filling the world around you with color, warmth, and an boundless love for everything that grows. 

Now, propelled by the violent beauty of gunpowder and fire, your spirit travels higher than any root could ever reach. I imagine you soaring past the stars, your eyes wide with wonder, searching the infinite dark for cosmic gardens yet unseen. Are you looking for strange, celestial flowers, tended by alien pollinators hovering in the dust of nebulae? Or perhaps, as you climb through the void, you are searching for a way back to your own past—tracing the original threads of your journey before you were ever transplanted to distant shores.

Below, the dramatic pyrotechnic spectacle slowly reaches its crescendo and begins to fade. The blinding flash of white and gold yields to a faint drifting haze; the fiery ladder burns down to a charred, smoking skeleton, and the great white balloon that held it aloft deflates against the morning sky. On the ground, the artist cheers, his face illuminated by a phone screen as he celebrates the successful performance with his own hundred-year-old grandmother, reaching across the miles to share his gift of fire and love.

Tell me, Grandmother—did you feel the rush of it? Did you experience the full majesty of that wondrous, fleeting journey into the stars? The fire has cooled now, and the sky is quiet once more. Take the peace of the cosmos with you, fold yourself back into the gentle dark, and return to your rest. Sleep peacefully.

Here is an expanded narrative poem based on your summary.

***

### The Ladder Made of Fire

**I. The Loom of Blood**

She carried two maps beneath her skin,
a collision of worlds she was forced to reconcile:
one shore of cold pine and marble pale,
the other of monsoon soil, ginger, and beaten gold.
All her life, she walked the fault line between them,
belonging fully to neither, translating her sorrow
into silent recipes and folded linen.
When her breathing finally slowed to a thread and snapped,
she left behind a house filled with half-translated prayers,
and a grief that felt too tangled for a simple grave.
How do you bury a woman whose roots stretched across oceans,
whose heritage was a quiet, restless sea?

**II. The Ignition**

Tonight, we do not scatter her ashes in the earth.
Instead, we lift our eyes to the dark canopy off the coast,
where Cai Guo-Qiang has anchored a miracle to the clouds.
A single fuse crackles—a white-hot hiss slicing through the dusk—
and the sky takes fire.
A five-hundred-meter ladder of flame ignites,
suspended by an unseen balloon, floating toward the cosmos.
It is a spine of sulfur and brass, a burning trellis of light.
In the violent, beautiful roar of gunpowder,
her spirit recognizes the medium:
neither white nor brown, but pure, roaring illumination.
Fire does not ask for papers; fire does not demand a single name.

**III. The Ascent**

She steps onto the lowest rung of sparks.
With every step upward, the weight of her earthly division sloughs away.
The deafening crackle of fireworks becomes a choir of ancestors,
cheering her climb up the golden steps.
The heat burns off the old pain—
the quiet rejections, the fractured dialects, the split heart.
As she ascends, the rungs glow hotter, brighter,
illuminating the deep indigo of the stratosphere.
She is no longer torn between two halves;
she is the bridge itself, incandescent and whole.

**IV. The Collapse**

Then comes the quiet logic of the flame.
The gunpowder consumes itself; the golden rungs burst, flicker, and die.
The charred skeleton of the ladder twists in the high winds,
crumbles, and rains down toward the dark ocean in soft, harmless ash.
The roar subsides into an overwhelming stillness.
The sky swallows the smoke.
The physical bridge is gone, burnt to cinders,
falling back to the sea that once separated her worlds.

**V. The Celestial Orchard**

But she has already stepped off the top rung.
Above the smoke, where the atmosphere turns to crystal silence,
she enters a garden hidden beyond the constellations.
Here, the stars grow like heavy, luminous fruit on branches of dark glass—
dragon fruit glowing with silver seeds, persimmons of pure amber light,
pomegranates bursting with tiny nebulae.
She reaches out and harvests the sky,
planting her complex roots in cosmic soil that welcomes all of her.
There is no division here, only sweetness and infinite space.

**VI. Closure**

Down on the darkened shore, the smoke clears from our eyes.
The night is cold again, but the heavy ache in my chest has loosened its grip.
I look up at the dark where the burning ladder just stood,
and for the first time since her passing, the silence feels complete.
She has found her orchard.
And below, standing in the quiet dark,
so have I.

For months, Cai and Guo worked in the quiet hush of the mountain valley. Cai was the visionary of light, sketching patterns of spark and flame on recycled parchment, while Guo was the master of form, measuring fuse lengths and constructing bamboo frameworks with patient precision. Together, they were preparing a grand, ephemeral spectacle—a firework installation designed to paint the night sky and celebrate the turn of the season.

When the festival night finally arrived, the darkness erupted. Crimson trails slashed through the clouds, and cascades of shimmering gold rained down upon the valley, echoing off the ancient stone hills. For a few breath-taking minutes, the heavens belonged entirely to their creation. 

Yet the true beauty of their work revealed itself only **after**. 

**After** the final burst of thunder dissolved into the mountain silence, and **after** the thick clouds of fragrant smoke drifted away on the midnight breeze, a profound quiet settled over the crowd. **Cai** stood at the edge of the firing field, his face brushed with ash, gazing up into the empty, starry expanse where their art had just lived. Beside him, **Guo** set down his tools and looked out over the valley, watching the soft glow of lanterns as the villagers slowly walked home, their faces still lit with wonder.

They both knew that firework art is fleeting by design. But in the quiet aftermath, **Cai** turned to **Guo** with a smile, understanding that the spectacle hadn't truly ended. The light was gone, but the memory of the warmth remained long **after** the fire had faded.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal prose poem addressing a deceased grandmother, using Cai Guo-Qiang's *Sky Ladder* fireworks installation as a vehicle for her soul ascending into the afterlife. Incorporate themes of gardening, her Anglo-Indian identity, and a traumatic fall.
counterfactuals.output:
Tonight, Nan, we set fire to the sky so you can un-fall. Remember the kitchen terrazzo, slick with damp tea leaves and morning light? The sudden, wicked betrayal of gravity, the sound of your hip snapping like a dry briar under winter’s boot. You dropped into the floorboards as if the earth had swallowed its own promise, your body folding like bruised linen. But here, in the dark salt flats of the night, gravity is only a suggestion we burn away.

A giant white lung of a helium balloon tugs a grid of hemp and gunpowder into the stratosphere. We strike the match. The fuse sings its hot, acrid lullaby—a scent of sulfur, crushed coriander, and burnt ozone. *One.* The lowest rung catches light, a sudden horizontal bloom of golden sparks. *Two.* The light leaps upward, a shining bamboo stake pushed deep into the black loam of midnight. It is a trellis made of pure combustion, climbing higher than the railway colonies of your youth, higher than the telegraph wires that carried your secret, hybrid heart between Kolkata and Kent.

You step onto the fire. Your bare soles, stained with the red dust of the Deccan and the dark earth of your potting shed, do not char. You carry your chipped enamel watering can, the one filled with rainwater and crushed mint. You were always a creature spliced from two gardens, Nan: your right hand pruning English sweet peas, your left hand coaxing violent, scarlet gulmohar to burst from sun-baked clay. You wore lace collars over skin the color of tea softened with evaporated milk, humming hymns in a dialect of monsoon rain and Victorian silver. 

Up you climb, step by golden step. As the rungs ignite in sequence—a ladder of controlled explosions ascending into the void—the jagged fault line in your pelvis begins to mend, sealed with molten brass and starlight. The terrible drop is reversed; this is the slow, glowing spooling-back of your descent. The pain that pinned you to the hospital bed unravels into light. At the fifty-second rung, where the air turns to frost, you pause to toss cuttings of starry night-jasmine into the dark. They do not fall; they float, taking root in the clouds like luminous water lilies.

The sky ladder burns its brief, magnificent spine into the atmosphere, a glowing seam stitching our mud to your eternity. Below, we breathe in the floating smoke of your chiffon sari. At the top of the blaze, where the rungs dissolve into open space, there are no wet tiles, no slick thresholds, no earth to betray you. You step off the last step of fire into an unmapped garden, sink your healed hands into the dark matter, and finally, effortlessly, bloom.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poetic eulogy for an Anglo-Indian grandmother who died after falling down the stairs on Guy Fawkes night. Imagine her climbing a ladder of gunpowder into space, blending imagery of black roses, planets, and fireworks.
counterfactuals.output:
Remember, remember, the fifth of November,
When the chilly night air was a bright, dying ember.
They say that she fell on the stairs made of oak,
But I saw her vanish in crimson and smoke.
Our Nana, our queen of two distant shores,
Left the warm, carpeted domestic floors,
Not broken or bowed by the gravity’s grace,
But launched like a rocket directly to space.

An Anglo-Indian jewel of velvet and lace,
With the scent of cardamom and cold English rain,
She carried dark heritage, fierce and untamed,
A beauty that couldn't be tethered or tamed.
She stepped on the stair, but her foot found a spark,
A fuse running upward through bone-chilling dark.

She didn't tumble—she climbed up the night,
On a ladder of gunpowder, sulfur, and light!
Each rung was a Catherine wheel, spinning in gold,
A story of fire that her ancestors told.
With a thunderous cheer from the bonfires below,
She rose through the sky in an amber-lit glow,
Leaving behind her the Earl Grey and silk,
Riding a comet through rivers of milk.

Higher she went, past the clouds and the birds,
To a silence too magnificent ever for words.
Her sari trailed behind her in shimmering arcs,
Sewn with the glitter of mortar-shell sparks.
Up where the air turns to velvet and frost,
Where nothing is broken, and nothing is lost.

Now she walks through the galaxies, weightless and free,
Past the pale, glowing rings of a sapphire-lit sea.
Near Jupiter’s moons, in the shadow of Mars,
She is planting black roses among all the stars.
Dark, velvety petals that drink in the night,
Stippled with stardust and meteorite light.

So do not mourn Nana, or pity her flight,
She didn't die falling—she ignited the night.
Whenever November unleashes its bloom,
And fireworks shatter the late-autumn gloom,
Look up at the cosmos, where the dark rose reposes:
She is climbing her ladder of fire and roses.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you write a piece of elegiac creative writing that connects contemporary pyrotechnic art—specifically Cai Guo-Qiang's burning ladder held up by a hot air balloon—with grief for a loved one who loved to garden?
counterfactuals.output:
You understood the geometry of climbing long before I ever saw the sky set on fire. 

In the late spring, your hands were always stained with dark, damp earth, the rich detritus of leaf-mold and bone meal. You would push wooden stakes into the ground, weaving hemp twine between them to guide the sweet peas and the clematis. *“They just need a little encouragement,”* you would say, tucking a stray green tendril around the wood, teaching it how to pull itself out of the dirt, how to reach toward a sun it couldn’t yet see. You spent a lifetime tending to things that took their time, bound by the slow, stubborn rhythm of root and rain.

Now, the garden is quiet, overgrown at the edges, and I am left holding the empty shears. 

I watched a video of Cai Guo-Qiang’s *Sky Ladder* late last night, sitting in the dark room you used to fill with starting trays and seed packets. I thought of you instantly. He built a grid of rope and wire, five hundred meters long, woven with gunpowder and fuse, tethered to a white hot-air balloon that drifted up into the grey dawn of Quanzhou. When he struck the match, it was not an explosion; it was an ascension. 

It was a trellis made of light.

Fire, usually so wild and consuming, became a plant in fast-forward. A single spark bit the bottom rung and shot upward, a golden stem bursting into a grid of blazing blossoms. Step by step, light climbed light. It clawed its way past the shoreline, past the clouds, blazing a blinding, temporary highway into the vault of the heavens. It was a bridge built out of sheer yearning, constructed to touch the invisible. Cai made it for his grandmother, to connect his home to the cosmos. I watched it burn and wept for the miles of empty blue between you and me.

How you would have marveled at that audacity. You, who spent hours on your knees helping vines struggle toward the light, would have understood the desperate, beautiful impulse to build a ladder out of fire just to check on what lies above us. 

Your whole life was a quieter version of that same art. Every tulip bulb pressed into the dark October frost was a fuse lit in reverse—a secret stored in the earth, waiting to explode into color when the world was ready. But grief is a garden where nothing grows fast enough. I want the pyrotechnic magic. I want to light a spark at the base of this empty space you left behind and watch a ladder of burning rungs tear through the sky, climbing straight to wherever you are now. I want to climb up through the smoke, past the cold air, just to hand you the secateurs one last time.

The tragedy of the sky ladder, of course, is that it can only last for a moment. The gunpowder burns through its own structure. The rungs ignite, glow fiercely against the dawn, and then snap into drifting embers. The balloon pulls away. The light dies, leaving only a ghost-line of grey smoke hanging in the atmosphere before the wind dissolves it completely.

It fell back to earth. Everything comes back to the earth.

This morning, I went out to your garden bed. The dirt was cold and dark, smelling of sulfur and damp stone after an autumn rain. I looked at the blackened soil, and I realized that fire and earth are not enemies—they are just different ways of returning. The burned ladder leaves behind ash, and ash is only potassium, only food for the soil, waiting for spring.

You are no longer the vine climbing into the light. You have become the air, the dark earth, the secret strength inside the seed. But tonight, when I close my eyes, I do not see you buried under six feet of loam. I see a spark striking the bottom of the sky. I see five hundred meters of golden flame climbing straight up into the dark. And I see you at the top, bending over the light, tending to the stars like morning glories.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a surreal, second-person narrative poem where the speaker envisions their dead grandmother climbing Cai Guo-Qiang’s Sky Ladder. Contrast her identity as a mixed-race woman transplanted to Britain with cosmic imagery of stars, tomatoes, soot, and light, ending with the real-life detail of Cai's own grandmother watching the event on a cell phone.
counterfactuals.output:
You watch her step off the wet clay of a Yorkshire allotment, 
leaving behind the cold grey drizzle of an island 
that always held her at arm’s length. 
Your grandmother—forged of two hemispheres, 
half-monsoon heat, half-industrial soot, 
her skin the dark honey of an empire’s crosscurrents—
places a worn leather shoe onto the first rung of wire.

Below her, the ignition strikes. 
Cai Guo-Qiang’s *Sky Ladder* catches fire, 
a five-hundred-meter spine of sulfur and silk 
hung from a giant white balloon in the morning blue. 
The gold fuse crackles like a million dry cicadas, 
and you watch her climb into the burning air.

She does not burn. Instead, the coal-smoke of post-war chimneys,
the decades of damp wool and quiet, polite rejections, 
slough off her arms like ash. 
In her apron pocket, she carries three ripe allotment tomatoes—
red, heavy globes bursting their skins in the thin atmosphere,
their seeds scattering out into space 
like hot solar flares, pulsing beside constellations.

Up she goes, past the altitude of birds, 
bridging the distance between her transplanted English soil 
and the infinite dark. 
The soot on her fingers turns to stardust; 
the light of the climbing fire illuminates her hair,
unbraiding the borders of her blood until she is neither foreign 
nor native, but pure, incandescent altitude.

And somewhere on the curve of the same earth, 
thousands of miles from where your vision takes flight, 
a hundred-year-old woman sits in a small bedroom in Quanzhou. 
Too frail to stand on the beach, 
she gazes into the illuminated rectangle of a cell phone screen 
held steady by a relative’s hand. 

Through that tiny window of glass—
smaller than an open palm, bright with streaming pixels—
she watches the fire ascend into the heaven of her grandson’s mind, 
while you watch your grandmother reach the top rung, 
stepping lightly off the light, and into the stars.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a short, evocative piece combining the following elements: Cai Guo-Qiang's Sky Ladder, an Anglo-Indian grandmother's skeleton, hybrid black roses, Guy Fawkes night, and a journey into the cosmos.
counterfactuals.output:
The fifth of November smelled of cordite, wet earth, and roasted sugar. Across the yard, bonfires crackled, sending orange embers to dance against the chill autumn dark, but in the center of the frosted lawn stood a quiet, impossible garden. 

There, rooted in rich loam, bloomed hybrid black roses—velvet petals so dark they seemed to drink the moonlight, bred to turn the shade of bruised plums at the edge of cold weather. Embedded among their thorned stems lay the skeleton of my grandmother. She had been Anglo-Indian, a delicate bridge between two worlds, her life a song of turmeric and damp fog, tea leaves and brass. Now, her ivory ribs formed a birdcage beneath the obsidian blossoms, cradling the dark earth.

Suddenly, a wire tautened against the vault of the atmosphere. 

A modern alchemy ignited. Up high, suspended by a high-altitude balloon, Cai Guo-Qiang’s *Sky Ladder* caught its spark. A fuse of gunpowder tore through the gloom, blazing rung by fiery rung into the troposphere. It was a trellis of golden flame, bridging the wild, pagan smoke of Guy Fawkes night with the quiet void above.

As the ladder climbed, the heat washed downward. The black roses sighed, releasing their perfume—a heady mix of damask, spice, and scorched sugar—as their petals caught the updraft. 

Then, the skeleton moved. 

Bone by porcelain bone, lifted by the thermal draft of sulfur and memory, she rose from her bed of dark flowers. Her spine unfurled like a chain of starlight. Hitching her fragile, gleaming ribs to the burning rungs of light, she began her ascent. Up she climbed, leaving behind the crackle of earthbound effigies and the smell of autumn chill, stepping over fiery rungs of golden spark.

Higher than the clouds, higher than the ash, the rose petals followed her in a swirling, dark nebula. My grandmother climbed past the sky into the vast, silent cosmos—an Anglo-Indian silhouette woven of bone and fire, stepping into the infinite dark, heading home to the stars.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
